Beneficial Properties of Bromelain

Summary, evaluation, and appraisal of Hikisz and Bernasinska-Slomczewska, Nutrients 2021;13:4313

Source type
Narrative literature review

Scope warning. This is a secondary narrative review. It is useful for mechanism mapping and reference discovery. It does not establish a current clinical indication, dose, or treatment recommendation for bromelain.

One-page synthesis

The review presents bromelain, a cysteine protease mixture from pineapple, as a biologically active compound with reported anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, fibrinolytic, antiplatelet, antimicrobial, and anticancer effects. The evidence base is mixed. It includes biochemical studies, cell systems, animal and ex vivo models, human tissue experiments, small clinical reports, and older clinical observations. The review also discusses bromelain absorption, safety, enzyme stability, wound debridement, osteoarthritis, postoperative symptoms, and potential use alongside antibiotics.

The most useful part of the paper is its map of mechanisms and citations. Table 1 groups inflammatory and immune targets. Figure 1 and Table 2 organize proposed anticancer mechanisms. The COVID-19 section extends these mechanisms to SARS-CoV-2 entry, inflammatory signaling, coagulation, and the bradykinin system. The paper itself gives the key boundary: anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity had not been tested in vivo in animal or human models, and clinical cancer evidence was sparse. That makes the stronger therapeutic language hypothesis-generating rather than practice-ready.

Verdict: Skim deeply. Read the methods, Tables 1 and 2, Figures 1 and 2, the clinical-application section, and the COVID-19 limitation. Use the 246-reference bibliography to locate primary studies. Do not use this review alone for clinical treatment decisions.

Review methods

The authors searched PubMed for "bromelain" alone or with cancer, inflammation, cardiovascular diseases, coagulation, fibrinolysis, medicine, and SARS-CoV-2 virus. Included articles were in English and published before 1 October 2021. Relevance was screened by title and abstract, followed by full-text evaluation.

No PRISMA-style study flow, complete reproducible search string, second database, duplicate screening process, risk-of-bias tool, evidence-certainty framework, or meta-analysis is reported. The review therefore cannot tell the reader how many records were found, excluded, or weighted, and it does not formally distinguish stronger human evidence from weaker mechanistic evidence.

Section condensation

Biochemical characterization

The paper distinguishes stem and fruit bromelain and summarizes differences in molecular weight, optimal pH and temperature, extract composition, proteolytic activity, and industrial use. It cites animal toxicity data with a reported lethal dose above 10 g/kg, oral absorption estimates of about 40% functionally intact bromelain in rat blood, and a reported half-life of 6 to 9 hours. The authors also mention unpublished HUVEC data without cytotoxicity at up to 50 ug/mL.

Safety discussion is mixed. Older clinical reports are described as showing few adverse effects, but the paper notes possible tachycardia with long-term use in people with hypertension and IgE-mediated allergy, especially in people allergic to pineapple. These safety claims are not pooled or quantified.

Cardiovascular disease, coagulation, and fibrinolysis

The review describes antiplatelet, fibrinolytic, and anticoagulant actions, including reduced platelet aggregation, increased plasmin generation, fibrin degradation, and changes in prostaglandin signaling. It also reports a concentration-dependent dual coagulation effect in one cited study, with procoagulant effects at low concentrations and anticoagulant effects at high concentrations.

Clinical and preclinical examples include a 73-patient thrombophlebitis report and an isolated rat-heart ischemia-reperfusion model. The review describes symptom improvement in the former and improved ventricular function and aortic flow in the latter. These examples are not sufficient to define a cardiovascular indication or dose.

Antimicrobial activity

The paper covers diarrhea models, antibiotic adjunct use, anthelmintic activity, antifungal activity, and antibacterial effects. It reports 35% to 62% reductions in bacterial toxin secretion in animal diarrhea models and describes higher antibiotic concentrations in animal and human reports when bromelain was coadministered. It also reviews bromelain-capped nanoparticle drug-delivery experiments.

The evidence is heterogeneous and often preclinical. The authors themselves note that anthelmintic activity is weaker in vivo than in vitro and that mechanisms for altered drug absorption are not fully understood.

Inflammation and immunomodulation

Cell and animal models suggest suppression of IL-6, IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, NF-kappaB, MAPK signaling, COX-2, and iNOS under inflammatory stimulation. The review also describes degradation of leukocyte surface molecules involved in migration and activation. In IBD models, the cited work includes IL-10-deficient mice and human colonic biopsy organ cultures.

The authors frame bromelain as context-dependent rather than uniformly immunosuppressive. In resting or differently activated immune systems, they describe increased T-cell proliferation and other stimulatory effects. Table 1 is the clearest evidence map for this section.

Anticancer properties

The cancer section is mechanistic and preclinical. It groups findings around apoptosis, cell-cycle arrest, autophagy, reactive oxygen species, and combination therapy. Models include breast, melanoma, epidermoid, leukemia, lymphoma, gastrointestinal, colorectal, hepatic, pancreatic, sarcoma, mesothelioma, and oral cancer systems. Figure 1 and Table 2 consolidate the proposed pathways and model-specific findings.

The source explicitly states that existing clinical trials provide little information on bromelain antitumor activity. That statement should control interpretation. Cell-line responses and tumor-model effects do not establish clinical efficacy.

Potential clinical applications

The review discusses chronic rhinosinusitis, postoperative edema and pain, enzymatic burn debridement, osteoarthritis, musculoskeletal recovery, and allergic sensitization. The debridement section is clinically notable because it includes both claimed benefit and a safety counterpoint. Cited studies report low selectivity and toxicity to viable human skin cells at high concentrations for bromelain-based NexoBrid.

For osteoarthritis and exercise recovery, the paper often discusses multi-ingredient regimens. Attribution to bromelain alone is therefore uncertain. Comparative dosing and effect estimates are not synthesized.

COVID-19 hypothesis

The review cites VeroE6-cell work in which bromelain affected ACE2, TMPRSS2, spike protein, viral binding, and viral RNA. It also cites bromelain plus acetylcysteine experiments and molecular docking studies. Figure 2 links those findings to inflammation, coagulation, fibrinolysis, platelet aggregation, and bradykinin pathways.

The paper then proposes supportive or prophylactic use in COVID-19. The same paper states that efficacy had not been tested in vivo in animal or human models. The therapeutic proposal therefore rests on preclinical and in silico evidence plus extrapolation from other bromelain effects.

Conclusions and future work

The authors conclude that bromelain has broad medical potential but that its mechanism remains incompletely understood. They identify instability under acidic conditions, gastric proteases, chemicals, organic solvents, and heat as practical barriers and call for better purification, stabilization, and production methods.

The conclusion is more confident than the review method can support for clinical efficacy. The strongest defensible use of the paper is as a structured hypothesis and citation map.

Evaluation and appraisal

5/10

Relevance

Useful as a broad map of bromelain pharmacology and cited literature, but much of the evidence is preclinical and outside routine clinical pharmacy decisions.

Evidence basis. Broad coverage of cardiovascular, inflammatory, infectious, cancer, wound, musculoskeletal, and COVID-19 topics.

Main limit. The paper does not answer a focused clinical question.

What would change it. A focused clinical question with current comparative human evidence would raise this score.

5/10

Novelty

The 2021 review gathers a wide set of mechanistic and translational claims, but much of the contribution is synthesis rather than new data.

Evidence basis. The paper links biochemical, inflammatory, coagulation, antimicrobial, cancer, and SARS-CoV-2 hypotheses.

Main limit. No original prospective clinical study or quantitative synthesis is presented.

What would change it. New primary data or a systematic synthesis with reproducible evidence grading would raise this score.

3/10

Method strength

The review searched one database with listed keywords and a date and language cutoff, but gives no reproducible full search string, screening counts, duplicate review, risk-of-bias process, or evidence grading.

Evidence basis. Methods section reports PubMed, search terms, English language, pre-1 October 2021 cutoff, title/abstract relevance screening, and full-text review.

Main limit. Narrative selection methods leave substantial risk of selective inclusion and uneven weighting.

What would change it. A registered systematic-review protocol, multi-database search, dual screening, risk-of-bias assessment, and transparent study flow would raise this score.

3/10

Evidence strength

The article summarizes many in vitro, animal, ex vivo, and small clinical reports without formal weighting, pooling, or certainty assessment.

Evidence basis. Tables 1 and 2 and the section summaries cite a wide experimental base.

Main limit. The source itself states that cancer clinical trials provide little information and that anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity had not been tested in vivo.

What would change it. Consistent, well-controlled human trials with effect estimates and uncertainty would raise this score.

3/10

External validity

Findings span many models and diseases, but the heterogeneity makes translation to patients uncertain.

Evidence basis. Human tissue and some clinical observations appear alongside cell, animal, ex vivo, and in silico studies.

Main limit. Dose, formulation, target population, and clinical endpoint consistency are often missing.

What would change it. Replicated human studies using standardized bromelain preparations and clinically meaningful outcomes would raise this score.

3/10

Implementation value

The paper is useful for reference mining and mechanism mapping, not for treatment selection or dosing.

Evidence basis. It identifies candidate uses, mechanisms, safety concerns, and 246 references.

Main limit. It does not provide a practice-ready regimen, comparative effectiveness framework, or evidence certainty.

What would change it. Current guidelines, product-specific dosing data, and high-quality comparative trials would raise this score.

Practice boundary. Do not use this review alone to start bromelain for cardiovascular disease, infection, cancer, osteoarthritis, or COVID-19. It does not provide the quality, comparative evidence, dosing standardization, or current-practice verification needed for that use.

Use and next steps

Best use

Reference mining, mechanism mapping, and identifying specific primary studies worth retrieving. The 246-reference queue is the practical output.

Do not use for

Current treatment recommendations, dosing, comparative effectiveness, or evidence certainty. Those require direct primary-study review and current guideline or regulatory verification.

High-value follow-up

Prioritize human trials and clinically relevant studies behind the thrombophlebitis, antibiotic-adjunct, wound-debridement, osteoarthritis, and exercise-recovery claims. For COVID-19, separate cell and in silico papers from any later human evidence.

Confidence in appraisal

High for the review-level appraisal because the full 36-page PDF, both figures, both tables, methods, conclusions, and bibliography were inspected. Low for any claim about the underlying primary studies until those papers are read directly.

Coverage and provenance

All 36 PDF pages were rendered and text-extracted. Pages 1 to 26 contain the review body and disclosures. Pages 27 to 36 contain 246 numbered references. Two figures and two tables were reconciled. No supplement was present in the retrieved folder.

ATOM structural validation used the supplied literature(1).py. Sufficiency validation used literature_atoms(1).py. Serialization was checked against literature_atom.schema.json. The README governed workflow intent and the example atom was illustrative only. SEA used summary-evaluation-appraisal-protocol-v4-compact.md as the governing file. Its internal heading says Integrated Compact v3. The supplied v3 HTML remained historical reference. large-source-ATOM-SEA.md supplied large-source batching rules. unslop.skill.md controlled prose style.

No external web verification was performed because @VERIFY was not activated. The paper is appraised as the supplied 2021 source, not as current clinical guidance.
